name: three

sources: Cunliffe, Barry. The Ancient Celts. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997), 187.
Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989, 169.
Powell, T. G. E. The Celts. London: Thames and Hudson, 1980, 154+.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Three is a significant and powerful number for the Celts. It mattered on the continent and on the islands. Only the number five appears more often in myth and ritual. The number itself was sacred. Anything that came in three parts stood for this religious value. In Wales the short poems called the Triads carry a great deal of myth. In Ireland the stories show kings and heroes suffering the threefold death. Many Celtic divinities appear three at a time. The Deae Matres are the mother goddesses of Gaul. The triple-horned bull appears in Britain. Triplicity often seems a way to strengthen a figure. Goddesses are most often tripled, as in the Morrigan, Macha, and Brigit. Gods are sometimes raised into a trinity too. The number three is also read as a full cycle. That cycle is past, present, and future, and mother, father, and child.

okr.objective: Record the sanctity of the number three.
key_results: Three is sacred and few numbers surpass it in mythology
Anything in three parts carries the religious value
Divinities such as the Deae Matres appear in triplicate
